summary: Discovery focused on reliability and incident tolerance. Pegasus has strict latency SLOs for payment authorization and needs multi-region failover with predictable fallbacks. Discussed Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, fallback policies (model variant, region, degraded QoS), KV/prefix caching, and SLAs. Next steps: pricing, security docs, SE-led benchmark in staging.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Morris (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (Pegasus - Head of Platform), Aisha Gomez (Pegasus - SRE Lead), Ben Cho (Pegasus - VP Product)
Links shared: Redwood reliability deck (link), dedicated sizing spreadsheet (link placeholder), SOC2 summary (link)

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh i'll do a 2 minute intro - i'm samir, i run enterprise for the payments vertical at redwood, and with me is lena, our systems engineer who will run the deep bits later.
[00:18] Mark: thanks samir, excited to chat, we've been evaluating a couple of options and reliability is the big gating factor for us.
[00:27] Lena: hi all, quick clarifier, are we talking about auth latency for card authorizations primarily or other flows like refunds and settlements?
[00:35] Ben: auth is the critical path, avg p99 needs to be < 150ms for user visible flows, and batch jobs can be looser.
[00:44] Aisha: and we want end-to-end authorization within 200ms including all network hops; also important is the behavior during incidents - how does the model routing degrade, and do we get deterministic fallbacks.

[01:05] Samir: perfect, that's helpful. so the high-level choices are hosted API, dedicated reserved capacity, or private/vpc on-prem. hosted is fastest to get going but we can talk through SLAs and fallbacks; dedicated gives you predictable capacity and isolation; private gives you full control including KMS in your VPC.
[01:30] Mark: one question up front - if a region has partial outage, what's the default routing? is it zone failover or full region failover, and how long to detect?
[01:40] Lena: good question - our control plane monitors health signals and we do active and passive health checks. detection is usually on the order of 10-30s depending on metrics; for critical routes we recommend multi-region active-active with edge routing. we also support automatic fallback policies: first line is to route to a compatible model variant in another region, second line is to degrade to a smaller quantized model, third line is to queue or shed low-priority requests.
[02:05] Aisha: when you say compatible model variant, can you give an example? like same architecture but quantized int8?
[02:12] Lena: yeah, exactly - same architecture but a quantized/32->8 bit run, or a distilled variant that preserves our quality threshold. we can define per-route policies so payments auth uses region failover to another high-throughput instance; less critical user-facing chat can fall back to a cheaper model.

[02:35] Ben: how is routing done? is it at DNS level or do you have a geo-aware proxy? we can't tolerate DNS TTL delays in some cases.
[02:44] Samir: we use smart routing in the control plane plus edge proxies. for hosted customers we have a traffic router that can do immediate reroute and we can integrate with customers' DNS for active-active. delta is that DNS-only failover is slower so we generally recommend our edge and health-checking to trigger switchover.

[03:10] Mark: ok, what about SLA - do you offer 99.9 or 99.95? and what does that cover (availability vs latency)?
[03:19] Lena: our standard hosted SLA today is 99.9 uptime for the API and latency SLOs are documented per model/route. for dedicated customers we can commit higher SLOs and tailor latency p95/p99 targets with reserved capacity. SLA credits are based on availability windows; for latency regressions we do root cause and can provide credits in some enterprise contracts.

[03:48] Aisha: one of our pain points is unpredictable cold-starts and kv cache misses - does redwood provide prefix/KV cache replication across regions?
[03:57] Lena: we do prefix and KV cache strategies; we currently keep hot cache local to the serving region for lowest latency but we can pre-warm or replicate critical prefixes to another region as part of a dedicated setup or via config in private deployments. there is a tradeoff in cost and memory. sometimes teams prefer a lightweight replicated cache for the very hot keys and rely on model fallbacks for the rest.

[04:30] Mark: would that mean duplicating KV across regions and added egress? we're sensitive to cross-region bandwidth.
[04:36] Lena: yes that creates cross-region replication costs; we can do selective replication only for the auth-prefixes which are small, so bandwidth is minimal. we also support async warm-up and traffic mirroring for rehearsals.

[05:05] Ben: what's your approach to canarying and rollbacks? we need automated safe rollouts because a mis-deployed model could increase latency or worse, change authorization behavior.
[05:15] Lena: rollouts support canary by traffic percentage and automatic fallback. if we detect increased error rates or latency we automatically roll traffic back to previous model/version. we also store evals and regression alerts tied to prompt sets - you can define acceptance criteria so a model won't be promoted unless it passes the checks.

[05:45] Aisha: curious about network level integration - for private/vpc, do you allow customer-controlled routing and do you support HSM/KMS integration for keys?
[05:55] Samir: yes, for private deployments the control plane is customer-managed and you can plug in your KMS/HSM. we have integrations for AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and can support bring-your-own HSM for on-prem. audit logs are shipped to your log sink and RBAC is enforced via SSO/SAML.

[06:20] Mark: we also asked legal about data residency - if traffic flows to another region during a failover, how is that logged and controlled?
[06:28] Lena: we can restrict which regions are eligible for failover for each route, and every routed request is logged with metadata (origin region, failover reason). logging can be exported to your SIEM. if you require strict residency we recommend private/dedicated where failover is limited to approved regions.

[06:50] Samir: do you have any existing on-prem infra or are you purely cloud?
[06:55] Mark: primarily multi-cloud (aws + gcp) and we run some critical infra in our own colo for PCI segregation.

[07:05] Lena: okay that explains some constraints - dedicated res pools in region + private connectors to colo could work.

[07:20] Ben: let's talk numbers - expected RPS at peak and typical token counts for an auth flow?
[07:27] Aisha: auth endpoint spikes to ~600 RPS per region at peak, p99 latency target 150ms. token size small - average 30-40 tokens per call but we do many concurrent parallel calls. also global volume is about 2M requests/day.

[07:50] Lena: thanks, that helps with sizing. given those numbers we'd recommend dedicated GPU pools with autoscaling and burst capacity; we can provide a sizing spreadsheet (i sent a simplified workbook) and then run a short benchmark in your staging region.

[08:12] Mark: how do you handle graceful degradation under overload? we cannot have authorizations fail silently.
[08:20] Lena: the plan is multi-layer: rate-limit and priority queueing at the edge, then model fallbacks (distilled / quantized), and if needed degrade to synchronous fallback to a cached decision service (if you have one) or return a deterministic fallback response with a fail-safe code so your systems can fallback to offline checks. we avoid returning hallucinated or ambiguous answers. for payments we recommend deterministic fallback responses or honoring cached allow/deny decisions.

[08:56] Samir: also worth noting we offer integrated traffic shaping so payment auth traffic can be pinned to high priority pools.

[09:05] Aisha: and observability - do we get token-level cost/latency breakdowns and traces? that's required for our monthly ops review.
[09:12] Lena: yes, console exposes per-route token breakdown, latency heatmaps, and traces. you can also stream traces and metics to your APM. for dedicated we can increase retention windows.

[09:32] Mark: what about runbooks and incident response - do you provide runbook templates for failover?
[09:38] Samir: yes, we provide runbooks and a runbook template we use with customers during onboarding; we can co-author runbooks covering DNS failover, control plane issues, and model regressions.

[09:50] Ben: one risk we have is model quality regression after a version swap - can we have automatic regression detection against a known testset?
[09:58] Lena: absolutely, we support eval sets and can block promotions if quality drops beyond thresholds. regression alerts can be sent to slack/pager and optionally auto-rollback.

[10:20] Mark: what's your RTO/RPO expectations for full region outage?
[10:25] Samir: that depends on deployment mode. for hosted, our operational playbook aims to failover within 30-90s for supported routes; dedicated/private can tune to lower detection windows and pre-warmed standby capacity to reduce RTO. RPO is near zero for stateful services but for caches it's eventual - we recommend strategies for critical keys replication if you need strict RPO.

[10:55] Aisha: do you have any customers in payments live on dedicated? curious references.
[11:00] Samir: yes, we've got a couple of mid-market payments customers on dedicated, and i can share anonymized latency/availability reports.

[11:10] Mark: are there any failure modes where all regions could be impacted - like control plane outage?
[11:16] Lena: control plane is separate and can be configured in private deployments; for hosted customers we have multi-region control plane redundancy, but in a severe universal cloud provider outage some regions could be affected. as mitigation we support local-only operating modes where the serving plane continues with cached config for a period if control plane is unreachable.

[11:44] Ben: ok good. what's the expected lead time for dedicated reserved pools? we may need commitment windows for capacity planning.

[11:52] Samir: typically 4-8 weeks to provision dedicated pools depending on GPU availability and region. we do offer burst capacity in the interim and pilot credits.

[12:05] Mark: and pricing model for dedicated vs hosted?

[12:10] Samir: hosted is usage-based (per token / per embedding), dedicated is reserved monthly contracts plus a per-token or compute metered overage model. i'll send a detailed sheet with examples for your RPS profile.

[12:28] Aisha: on the security front, we'll need SOC2, penetration test summary, and network diagrams - can you share?

[12:34] Samir: yes we will share SOC2 report and a redacted pen test summary; for private deployments we can provide a full network architecture and assume a security review cadence.

[12:48] Lena: small note on KV cache again - if you choose dedicated we can pre-warm caches and keep standby replicas in a secondary region which reduces failover latency to single-digit ms for hot keys.

[13:05] Ben: that sounds promising; our main concern is predictability and deterministic behavior during incidents.

[13:12] Mark: what are your guarantees on model output consistency when failing over to a different region or quantized model? slight change in decision logic could be problematic.

[13:20] Lena: we recommend using deterministic model variants for critical decisioning; also we provide a canary and eval step with your testset prior to promoting a variant. but small differences can exist between quantized vs fp32; that's why we often suggest a replicated fallback decision service or a hybrid approach where the model returns evidence and your rules engine makes final allow/deny call.

[13:50] Samir: to summarize from redwood's side - we can support multi-region active-active routing, configurable failover policies (region -> model variant -> queue), pre-warmed KV replication for hot keys, dedicated reserved pools for throughput with SLA tailoring, and private deployment for strict residency and KMS/HSM integration.

[14:18] Mark: next steps for us are a) review pricing, b) run a short benchmark in our staging region, c) security docs review.

[14:25] Samir: we'll action those. lena, can you lead the benchmark plan?

[14:29] Lena: yep i'll put together a test matrix - latency/throughput/failed-region sim and share by Friday.

[14:35] Aisha: i'll send our exact p99 targets and an example payload set.

[14:40] Ben: team, thanks. we'll expect the spreadsheet and SOC2 docs.

[14:46] Samir: great, i'll follow up with a summary and the links. thanks everyone.

[15:00] End call
